title: Views held lightly
hook: the raft: even good teachings are for crossing over, not for holding on to (MN 22)
tomorrow: The blind men and the elephant

segments.voice: Yesterday: worldly right view, and your line, deeds matter. Did you do one small thing as if it would ripen somewhere? Today closes the week. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

The raft story has come up more than once on this path. But the sutta it comes from has a darker opening. A monk named Arittha, whom the text calls a former vulture trainer, has decided that, as he understands the teaching, the things the Buddha called obstacles aren't really obstacles at all. The other monks can't talk him out of it. So the Buddha calls him in. Before the raft, there's a snake.
screen: `A MONK SURE OF HIS READING.` → `THE OTHERS CAN'T MOVE HIM.` → `BEFORE THE RAFT, A SNAKE.`

segments.voice: The sutta is the Simile of the Water Snake, number twenty-two in the Middle-Length Discourses. The Buddha says some people learn the teaching, but don't look into its meaning with wisdom. They learn it in order to criticize others, or to win debates. They're like a man looking for a water snake who grabs it by the tail. It turns and bites him. A teaching grabbed the wrong way can hurt the one who grabs it. Then the raft. A man comes to a wide river. This side is dangerous; the far side is safe; there's no ferry and no bridge. He gathers grass, sticks and branches, binds them into a raft, and paddles across. On the far bank he thinks: this raft was so useful, I'll lift it onto my head and carry it wherever I go. Would that be the right thing to do with a raft? No, say the monks. He should haul it up onto dry land, or set it adrift in the water, and go on his way. In the same way, the Buddha says, he has taught the Dhamma like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to. And he adds: you should let go even of good teachings, how much more of bad ones. It's said in a sutta that began with a monk gripping his own reading of the teaching. Views aren't useless. They're boats. And looking back over the week: seeing dependent arising as seeing the Dhamma, the four truths closed, eight spokes, right view as a lens, the three roots, worldly right view. Today's lesson holds all of them: carry them lightly.
screen: `ARITTHA'S WRONG GRASP.` · `A SNAKE GRABBED BY THE TAIL.` · `A RAFT ON THE FAR BANK.` · `LET GO EVEN OF GOOD TEACHINGS.` · then, large: `A RAFT, NOT A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hold one opinion loosely. Sit and settle. Bring to mind an opinion you hold firmly: about politics, a family matter, the right way to load a dishwasher. Feel how it sits in you, maybe a tightness, a readiness to argue. Now picture it as a raft: useful, built for a purpose. Without throwing it away, imagine setting it down on the bank for a moment. Notice how your hands feel. The bell holds the time.
Views held lightly. The teaching is a raft for crossing, not something to grasp like a snake by the tail, and not a house to live in.
Your line: a raft, not a house. Today, in one disagreement, ask yourself whether you're using your view to cross a river, or carrying it on your head. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many settings use the raft simile to remind students that teachings and views are tools for freedom, and some traditions, Zen among them, stress not clinging even to the words of the teaching.

pairs: a teaching grabbed the wrong way
a monk clinging to a wrong view
where the raft is left behind

myth: the raft story says teachings are useless
the raft got the man across; it's useful, just not for carrying on your head.
the same sutta warns against grabbing a teaching like a snake by the tail
learning it to criticize or win debates can bite the one who grabs it.
the Buddha says to let go even of good teachings
how much more, he adds, of bad ones.

fork.setup: you've crossed a dangerous river on a raft you built. you're on the safe bank. what do you do with the raft?
options: carry it on your head wherever you go.
haul it onto dry land, or set it adrift, and go on.
fork.reveal: the monks agree he should haul it ashore or set it adrift and go on; the Buddha says the Dhamma is like a raft, for crossing over, not for holding on to.

original.note: Pali kulla: a raft; the sutta speaks of the Dhamma as kullūpama, like a raft.

trapdoor: what you thought: the raft story means Buddhism doesn't take its teachings seriously.
what it means: teachings are serious tools for crossing, and grasping them wrongly can hurt.

what a scholar hears: MN 22 pairs the water-snake simile (alagadda) with the raft (kulla), aimed at Ariṭṭha, said to be a former vulture trainer, and adds dhammā pi vo pahātabbā pageva adhammā: even dhammas are to be let go, how much more non-dhammas.

sources.ref: MN 22 (Alagaddupama Sutta, the water snake and the raft)

notes: The raft has appeared many times in year one (e.g. days 45, 56–57, 330); today's angle is the water-snake half and Ariṭṭha. Keeper may judge repetition.
Ariṭṭha's former occupation (gaddhabādhipubba, 'formerly a vulture trainer'): confirm.
MN 22 paraphrased: confirm the snake simile's purposes (learning for criticizing others and winning debates) and the raft wording.

Editor review: Arittha's view corrected (MN 22 has him claim that, as he understands the Buddha's teaching, obstructions do not obstruct, not that he knows better than the teaching); 'leave it on the bank' corrected to MN 22's two options (haul it onto dry land or set it adrift), also in the fork; dropped the stock 'the sentence people sometimes forget' and the 'you've probably heard' opener; howItsDone no longer says 'every school'.
